definition: A REC is a separately tradable certificate proving that one megawatt-hour of electricity was generated by an eligible renewable resource and injected into a power grid; because electricity on a grid can't be traced back to its source once delivered, RECs exist as an electronic accounting mechanism to track and trade the 'renewable' attribute apart from the physical power itself.
core_idea: RECs decouple the claim of having used renewable energy from the physical electricity, allowing that environmental attribute to be created, traded, and sold independently of the underlying power delivery.
key_points: One REC certifies 1 MWh of generation from an eligible renewable source delivered to a grid
RECs exist primarily as electronic records, not physical goods
Trading/transfer of a REC happens separately from the electricity transaction
RECs exist because grid electrons can't be physically distinguished by generation source
relationships: REC markets primarily coexist with deregulated power markets
In regulated (monopoly utility) markets, renewable obligations are typically met via PPAs with renewable generators instead of REC purchases
trading_implications: A REC's value comes entirely from external compliance or voluntary demand, not from any physical energy property
caveats: A REC is not the electricity itself — an owner can hold the renewable claim without ever physically receiving power from that generator
